usage: 신청 + 하다 is the verb form
noun-noun compound for the open window
examples: 여기에서 카드를 신청해요.
I apply for a card here.
Simple frame: 신청하다 turns the noun into 'to apply for' + object 를.
인터넷으로 통장을 신청했어요.
I applied for a bankbook online.
Everyday errand: method 으로 + object + 신청하다 in past tense.
신청은 다음 주 금요일까지 받습니다.
Applications are accepted until next Friday.
Real counter notice: 신청 as the thing the office 받다 (accepts) within a deadline 까지.
nuance: 신청 is a Sino-Korean noun (申請, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') meaning a formal application or request you put in to an office, bank, or service — you are asking an authority to grant or process something. It overwhelmingly takes 하다 to become the verb 신청하다 ('to apply for'), and 신청서 is the physical form you fill in. Compare it carefully with 지원 (支援/志願): 신청 is the neutral 'put in a request' (카드를 신청하다 = apply for a card), while 지원 is 'apply to/for' a job or school where you are a candidate being selected (회사에 지원하다 = apply to a company). Also distinguish 접수, which is the office's act of RECEIVING and logging your 신청. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in any official or banking setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 지원 for everyday errands (it sounds like job-hunting) and forgetting that 신청 needs 하다 to act as a verb — 신청 by itself is only the noun, so 'I apply' is 신청해요, not bare 신청.

mistakes: Using 지원 for everyday requests like 'apply for a card' — 지원하다 implies competing for a job/school; for services and paperwork use 신청하다 (카드를 신청해요).

Confusing 신청 (your request) with 접수 (the office logging it) — you 신청하다, then the counter 접수하다; they are two sides of one transaction.

usage: to fill out an application form
에 marks where you sign on it
examples: 이 신청서를 써 주세요.
Please fill out this application form.
Simple frame: 신청서 as object of 쓰다 (write/fill in) with polite request.
신청서에 이름과 전화번호를 적어요.
I write my name and phone number on the application form.
Everyday: 에 marks the form as the surface you write 적다 the details onto.
신청서를 작성하신 후에 1번 창구에 제출해 주세요.
After completing the application form, please submit it at window 1.
Real counter instruction: formal 작성하다 + 제출하다 with the sequence 후에.
nuance: 신청서 is a Sino-Korean compound (申請書, 신청 'application' + 書 'document/writing') — the actual paper or digital FORM you complete to make a 신청. The 書 suffix is the same 'written document' element in 서류, 계약서 (contract), and 보고서 (report), so recognizing it helps you read official office vocabulary. Distinguish 신청서 (the specific application form) from the broader 서류 (any documents/paperwork) and from 양식 (the blank template/format itself): you grab the 양식, write on it, and it becomes your 신청서, which is one piece of 서류. The verbs that pair with it are formal: 작성하다 (fill out/complete) and 제출하다 (submit), rather than casual 쓰다/내다 — though 쓰다 and 내다 are fine in speech. Register is neutral-formal, standard at counters. The English-speaker pitfall is calling every document a 신청서: it is specifically an APPLICATION form, so a contract is 계약서 and general paperwork is 서류 — and remember the form-filling verb is 작성하다, not 만들다 (make).

examples: 서류가 더 필요해요.
I need more documents.
Simple frame: 서류 as subject of 필요하다 (to be needed).
은행에 가기 전에 서류를 챙겨요.
I gather the documents before going to the bank.
Everyday errand: 챙기다 (gather/pack) the papers ahead of the 전에 clause.
여권 사본 같은 필요한 서류를 모두 제출하셔야 합니다.
You must submit all the required documents, such as a passport copy.
Real procedure: 필요한 서류 (required documents) as object of formal obligation 제출하셔야 합니다.
nuance: 서류 is a Sino-Korean noun (書類, 書 'writing/document' + 類 'kind/category') meaning official documents or paperwork as a category — the bundle of forms, copies, and certificates a procedure demands. It is a collective, somewhat abstract term: 서류를 준비하다 = get your paperwork in order, covering many individual papers at once. Contrast it with 문서 (文書), which is 'a document' as a discrete file or record (often electronic or archival, e.g. an internal 문서), while 서류 evokes the practical stack you submit for an application. A single sheet is 종이 (paper) and one specific form is e.g. 신청서; 서류 is the umbrella. Natural collocations are 서류를 준비하다/챙기다/제출하다/접수하다 and 서류 심사 (document review). Register is neutral, ubiquitous at banks, immigration, and government offices. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 서류 as countable like 'a document' — Korean uses it as a mass/collective noun, so you rarely say 한 서류; for one item name the specific form (신청서 한 장) or use 문서 for a discrete record.

examples: 신분증 있으세요?
Do you have your ID?
Simple frame: the everyday counter question, 있다 + honorific 으세요.
통장을 만들 때 신분증이 필요해요.
You need an ID when opening a bankbook.
Everyday: 신분증 as subject of 필요하다 inside a 때 (when) clause.
본인 확인을 위해 신분증을 제시해 주시기 바랍니다.
Please present your ID for identity verification.
Real formal notice: 제시하다 with 위해 (for the purpose of) 본인 확인 (identity check).
nuance: 신분증 is a Sino-Korean compound (身分證, 身分 'social status/identity' + 證 'certificate/proof') — any official photo ID that proves who you are: a 주민등록증 (national ID), 운전면허증 (driver's license), or 여권 (passport) all count as a 신분증. The 證 'proof' suffix recurs in 학생증 (student ID), 자격증 (certificate), and 영수증 (receipt), so it flags 'certifying document'. Note the difference from 신분 alone, which is the abstract 'identity/social standing' (신분을 밝히다 = reveal one's identity), while 신분증 is the physical card. At banks and offices the set verbs are formal: 제시하다 (present) and 지참하다 (bring), with staff doing 확인하다 (verify); in speech 보여 주다 (show) and 가져오다 (bring) are natural. Register is neutral, indispensable for any errand. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 아이디 (a loanword that in Korean means a login USERNAME, not a physical ID) when you mean the card — for a photo identity card always use 신분증, and never confuse it with 카드 alone (which suggests a bank/credit card).

usage: 만들다 = the standard verb for opening one
정리 = bringing entries up to date
noun-noun: the account one's pay goes into
examples: 통장을 만들고 싶어요.
I want to open a bankbook.
Simple frame: 통장 as object of 만들다 with desire 고 싶다.
통장에 돈이 얼마나 있어요?
How much money is in the account?
Everyday: 통장에 (in the bankbook) as location of 돈 with 있다.
새 통장을 개설하려면 신분증과 도장이 필요합니다.
To open a new bankbook, you need an ID and a seal.
Real bank procedure: formal 개설하다 + intention 려면 listing required items with 과.
nuance: 통장 is a Sino-Korean noun (通帳, 通 'pass through/circulate' + 帳 'ledger/book') — the physical passbook that records deposits and withdrawals, and by extension the everyday word Koreans use for a bank account itself (통장을 만들다 = open an account). Here is the key contrast learners must master: 통장 is the tangible book / the account in casual speech, while 계좌 (計座) is the technical ACCOUNT NUMBER and the formal term used for transfers (계좌이체 = wire transfer, 계좌번호 = account number). So you 'open a 통장' but you 'transfer to a 계좌'. The verb for opening is colloquial 만들다 or formal 개설하다 (establish). Natural collocations: 월급 통장 (salary account), 통장 정리 (update the passbook), 통장 사본 (a copy of the passbook). Register is neutral, fully everyday. The English-speaker pitfall is using 계좌 where 통장 is natural and vice versa: to open the book say 통장을 만들다, but when giving someone your details for a transfer, you give your 계좌번호, not your 통장번호.

mistakes: Using 계좌 for the physical book/casual 'account' — you 통장을 만들다 (open a bankbook); 계좌 is the formal account/number used for transfers.
Saying 통장번호 for the number you give for a transfer — that is 계좌번호; 통장 is the book itself.
Using 열다 ('open' a door) to mean 'open an account' — the verb is 만들다 (make) or formal 개설하다 (establish).

usage: 알려 주다 = tell/inform someone of it
examples: 계좌번호를 알려 주세요.
Please tell me your account number.
Simple frame: 계좌번호 as object of 알려 주다 with polite request.
친구 계좌로 십만 원을 보냈어요.
I sent 100,000 won to my friend's account.
Everyday: 계좌로 (to the account) as destination of 보내다 (send).
급여는 등록된 계좌로 자동 이체됩니다.
Your salary is automatically transferred to the registered account.
Real notice: 계좌로 as destination of passive 이체되다 (be transferred), with 등록된 (registered).
nuance: 계좌 is a Sino-Korean noun (計座, 計 'count/reckon' + 座 'seat/position') meaning a bank account in the technical, financial sense — the entity identified by a 계좌번호 (account number) that money moves into and out of. It is the formal counterpart to 통장 (the physical passbook / casual word for account): banks, transfer screens, and official forms all say 계좌 — 계좌이체 (account transfer), 가상계좌 (virtual account), 계좌 개설 (account opening). The distinction is functional: you 통장을 만들다 (open the book) but you 입금하다 / 이체하다 to a 계좌, and you give your 계좌번호 for someone to pay you. The verb is 개설하다 (formal, 'establish') rather than 만들다 in official contexts. Register is neutral-formal, the standard term in any financial transaction. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing 계좌 and 통장: when transferring money or quoting the number, always use 계좌(번호); reserve 통장 for the passbook or casual 'I opened an account'. Also do not confuse 계좌 with 계산 (計算, calculation/paying a bill) — close-looking 한자 but different words.

Confusing 계좌 (account) with 계산 (paying/calculating a bill) — similar 한자 but 계산하다 means to settle a bill, not to bank.

usage: 확인되다 = it is verified as received
내역 = itemized record of incoming money
examples: 계좌에 오만 원을 입금했어요.
I deposited 50,000 won into the account.
Simple frame: 입금하다 with amount + 계좌에 as destination 에.
돈을 입금하면 문자가 와요.
When you deposit money, a text message comes.
Everyday: 입금하다 in a 면 (when/if) clause; deposit triggers an alert.
입금이 확인되는 대로 상품을 보내 드리겠습니다.
We will ship the item as soon as the deposit is confirmed.
Real transaction: passive 입금이 확인되다 with 는 대로 (as soon as) in formal commerce.
nuance: 입금 is a Sino-Korean noun (入金, 入 'enter' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money coming IN — depositing funds into an account, or money being received. It takes 하다 (입금하다 = to deposit/pay in) and pairs with 에 for the destination: 계좌에 입금하다. Its exact opposite is 출금 (出金, money going out / withdrawal), and the 入/出 pair is worth memorizing together, like 입구/출구 (entrance/exit). Distinguish 입금 from 송금 (送金, 'remitting/sending money', emphasizing the transfer ACROSS to another party) and from 이체 (移替, the account-to-account 'transfer' operation): when you pay a seller, you 입금하다 (the money enters their account) or 송금하다 (you send it); the bank's mechanism is 이체. Natural collocations: 입금 확인 (deposit confirmation), 입금 내역, 무통장 입금 (bankless/cash deposit). Register is neutral, everyday in shopping and banking. The English-speaker pitfall is using 저금 (saving up) or 예금 (a savings deposit/balance) for the act of paying in — those describe SAVING money, while 입금 is the transactional act of putting funds into an account right now.

Using 저금 or 예금 for 'pay this in' — 저금/예금 mean saving money; the act of depositing into an account is 입금하다.
Forgetting the destination particle — it is 계좌에 입금하다 (에 = into); using 로 here sounds off for the receiving account.

examples: 현금을 출금했어요.
I withdrew some cash.
Simple frame: 출금하다 with object 현금 (cash) in past tense.
통장에서 십만 원을 출금하려고 해요.
I'm going to withdraw 100,000 won from the account.
Everyday: 출금하다 with source 에서 + amount and intention 려고 하다.
하루 출금 한도는 백만 원으로 제한됩니다.
The daily withdrawal limit is capped at one million won.
Real bank rule: 출금 한도 as subject with 으로 제한되다 (be limited to).
nuance: 출금 is a Sino-Korean noun (出金, 出 'exit/go out' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money going OUT — withdrawing funds from an account. It takes 하다 (출금하다 = to withdraw) and, crucially, pairs with 에서 (the source) rather than 에: 계좌에서 출금하다 = withdraw FROM the account. It is the direct opposite of 입금 (入金, depositing), and learners should drill the 入/出 contrast plus the particle switch (입금은 '에', 출금은 '에서'). Near terms: 인출 (引出) is a more formal synonym for cash withdrawal seen on ATM screens and forms, while 출금 is the everyday word; 이체 (transfer) moves money to another account rather than taking it out as cash. Natural collocations: 출금 한도 (withdrawal limit), 자동 출금 (auto-debit), 출금 수수료 (withdrawal fee). Register is neutral, standard at ATMs and banks. The English-speaker pitfall is using 에 instead of 에서 with 출금 (the money LEAVES, so it is the source 에서), and confusing 출금 with 입금 — because the 한자 differ by only one character, mixing them up can send money the wrong way.

usage: 붙다 = a charge attaches to the transaction
noun-noun: the charge for sending money
examples: 수수료가 있어요?
Is there a fee?
Simple frame: the everyday counter question, 수수료 + 있다.
다른 은행으로 보내면 수수료가 붙어요.
If you send to another bank, a fee is added.
Everyday: 수수료가 붙다 (a fee attaches) inside a 면 condition about cross-bank transfers.
타행 이체 시 건당 오백 원의 수수료가 부과됩니다.
A fee of 500 won per transaction is charged for transfers to other banks.
Real bank notice: 수수료가 부과되다 (be levied) with 건당 (per case) and 시 (upon/when).
nuance: 수수료 is a Sino-Korean noun (手數料, 手數 'effort/handling' + 料 'charge/fee') meaning a service fee or commission — the charge a bank, agency, or service takes for handling a transaction (transfer fees, ATM fees, brokerage commission). The 料 'fee' suffix recurs in 요금 (utility/usage charge), 입장료 (entrance fee), 수업료 (tuition), so it flags 'a charge for ~'. Distinguish 수수료 from those siblings: 요금 is a usage charge for a service you consume (전기 요금 = electricity bill, 통화 요금 = call charges), 세금 (稅金) is a tax to the government, and 비용 (費用) is general 'cost/expense' — while 수수료 specifically is the HANDLING fee skimmed for processing your transaction. Natural verbs: 수수료가 들다/붙다/부과되다 (a fee is incurred/added/levied) and 수수료를 내다 (pay it). Register is neutral-formal, standard wherever transactions carry charges. The English-speaker pitfall is using 요금 or 비용 for a transaction commission — for the per-transaction handling charge at a bank or service, the precise word is 수수료, and remember it 'attaches' with 붙다 rather than being 'made'.

mistakes: Using 요금 for a bank commission — 요금 is a usage charge (전기 요금); the per-transaction handling fee is 수수료.
Calling it 세금 — 세금 is a government tax; a service's processing charge is 수수료, not a tax.
Saying 수수료를 만들다 — fees are not 'made'; they 들다/붙다/부과되다 (are incurred/added/levied), and you 내다 (pay) them.

usage: 등록 + 하다 = enter oneself/something on a register
examples: 여기에 이름을 등록해요.
I register my name here.
Simple frame: 등록하다 with object 이름 in present tense.
외국인 등록을 하러 출입국 사무소에 가요.
I'm going to the immigration office to do my alien registration.
Everyday: 외국인 등록 (alien registration) as object of 하다 with purpose 러.
수강 신청 후 등록금을 납부해야 등록이 완료됩니다.
Registration is complete only after you pay tuition following course sign-up.
Real procedure: passive 등록이 완료되다 (registration is completed) tied to 납부 (payment) condition.
nuance: 등록 is a Sino-Korean noun (登錄, 登 'record/ascend' + 錄 'register/record') meaning officially entering a person or thing onto a register or roll — enrolling, registering, recording in a system. It takes 하다 (등록하다 = to register) or 되다 (등록되다 = to be registered), and appears in 외국인 등록증 (alien registration card), 주민등록 (resident registration), 등록금 (registration/tuition fee), 등록 번호 (registration number). The contrast learners need is with 신청 and 접수: 신청 is REQUESTING something, 접수 is the office RECEIVING your request, and 등록 is the result of being formally ENTERED onto the official record — often you 신청 first, the desk 접수, and finally you are 등록 in the system. Compare also 가입 (加入, 'joining/subscribing' to a membership, service, or insurance — 보험 가입, 회원 가입), which is about becoming a MEMBER, whereas 등록 is about being recorded in a registry. Register is neutral-formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 등록 for joining a club or signing up for a service (that is 가입) and using 가입 for recording an official entry (that is 등록) — and remembering 등록 needs 하다/되다 to function as a verb.

Saying bare 등록 as a verb — add 하다 (등록해요) or 되다 (등록됐어요); 등록 alone is only the noun.

usage: 접수 + 하다 = lodge your application at the desk
되다 = the office has logged it
examples: 여기에서 접수하세요.
File it here. / Register here.
Simple frame: 접수하다 with honorific request at an intake desk.
오전에 서류를 접수했어요.
I filed the documents in the morning.
Everyday: 접수하다 with object 서류 in past tense — handed in and logged.
접수가 완료되면 접수 번호를 문자로 보내 드립니다.
Once your filing is complete, we send the reference number by text.
Real procedure: passive 접수가 완료되다 with the assigned 접수 번호 being sent.
nuance: 접수 is a Sino-Korean noun (接受, 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept') meaning the RECEIVING and logging of an application or document by an office — both the act of an institution taking your submission in, and (loosely) your act of handing it in at the 접수 창구 (intake window). It takes 하다 and 되다: from your side 서류를 접수하다 can mean 'submit/file', while 접수가 되다 / 접수되다 means 'it has been received/registered by them'. The crucial trio for learners: 신청 (you REQUEST) → 접수 (the office RECEIVES/logs it) → 처리 (處理, they PROCESS it). So 접수 sits in the middle, the moment your paperwork is officially accepted and assigned a 접수 번호. Distinguish it from 제출 (提出, the physical act of 'submitting/handing over' a document) — 제출 is the handing in, 접수 is the institution accepting and registering it. Register is neutral-formal, standard at hospitals, offices, and event desks (병원 접수 = hospital reception/check-in). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 접수 as plain 'submit' (that is 제출) and missing its 'be accepted/logged' meaning — 접수가 됐어요 means your application is now officially in the system, not merely handed over.

usage: 발급 + 받다 = receive an issued document
the charge to have it issued
examples: 여권을 발급받았어요.
I got a passport issued.
Simple frame: 발급받다 (receive issuance) with object 여권 in past tense.
증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
You can get the certificate from an automated issuing machine.
Everyday: 발급 in the compound 발급기 (issuing kiosk) with 뽑다 (print/pull) + ability.
카드를 분실하셨다면 재발급을 신청하셔야 합니다.
If you have lost your card, you must apply for a reissue.
Real procedure: 재발급 as object of 신청하다 under a 다면 (if) condition, formal obligation.
nuance: 발급 is a Sino-Korean noun (發給, 發 'issue/send out' + 給 'give/supply') meaning the official ISSUING of a document, card, or certificate by an authority — passports, ID cards, certificates, bank cards are all 발급. Crucially, it splits by direction: the OFFICE 발급하다 (issues), but YOU 발급받다 (receive the issuance) — so for your own errand the natural verb is 발급받다, not 발급하다 (which would mean you are the issuer). This 받다 pattern mirrors other 'receive an action' verbs. 재발급 (reissue) is the common compound when something is lost. Distinguish 발급 from 신청 and 등록: you 신청 (request) a document, the office 발급 (issues) it, after which you might be 등록 (recorded) somewhere. Compare also 교부 (交付), a more bureaucratic synonym for 'issue/hand over' seen in legal/government text, versus everyday 발급. Register is neutral-formal, standard at banks and government counters. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 발급하다 about getting your OWN document — that wrongly casts you as the issuing authority; to say 'I got X issued', use 발급받다.
